normalized.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: grow the software business, and reopen the question on four conditions
executive_summary: Quick commerce is growing fast, but neither incumbent makes money on an order – Zipcart loses $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 on each order (p. 4, 5)
At our customer sites' median, each order loses $6.17 after site costs – On order value alone, it would need a $63 basket to break even (p. 7–11)

Customers try the service, but few stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost – Only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month three – A retained customer repays its $38 cost only after about 15 months (p. 13, 14)

The plan breaches the 12-month runway floor even if everything goes right – The plan needs 1.3 times the cash we can spend above the floor – At median economics, nine stores would lose about $18M a year (p. 16, 17)

Scaling the software instead costs $0.8M a year and keeps grocers as customers – Late-stage grocers alone hold contracts worth 21% of today's ARR – A one-store pilot would spend $2.6M re-testing what we already know (p. 19–21)

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing fast, but neither incumbent makes money on an order
US quick-commerce grocery sales nearly tripled between 2022 and 2025, confirming that demand is real

claims.claim: US quick-commerce grocery sales nearly tripled between 2022 and 2025, confirming that demand is real
evidence: 2.8x GMV in 2025 as a multiple of 2022

claims.claim: Every year: growth ran between 38% and 44%, an average of 41.5% a year
Founders' claim: "growing over 40% a year" holds on the market data
What it measures: sales through all operators, not their profit

slides.title: Growth has not brought profit, as both incumbents lose money overall and on every order

claims.claim: Zipcart and QuickBasket lose a quarter to almost half of revenue at EBITDA
evidence: EBITDA margin 2025: Zipcart (national) -0.2583; QuickBasket (regional) -0.4571
Zipcart revenue $1,200M and EBITDA −$310M; QuickBasket revenue $210M and EBITDA −$96M (briefing pack, Table 2)

claims.claim: Each order loses money before any overhead is paid
evidence: Contribution per order 2025: Zipcart -1.9; QuickBasket -3.4
Operators' contribution definitions are not disclosed

claims.claim: QuickBasket, the regional operator closest to our model, closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025

slides.title: Unit economics
Only the founders' plan makes money per order; every set of inputs we have observed loses money after site costs

claims.claim: The evidence points to losses; only the forecast points to profit
evidence: Before site fixed costs: Columbus pop-up -6.2124; Customer-site median -2.6658; Best of each input 0.4933; Founders' plan 3.7686
After site fixed costs: Columbus pop-up -12.5725; Customer-site median -6.1666; Best of each input -1.7572; Founders' plan 2.0182

claims.claim: Columbus pop-up: our own test lost money on every input, from basket size to rider productivity
Customer-site median: the typical site of our 14 software customers loses money before rent is paid
Best of each input: even the best value of each input, taken from different sites, ends below zero after site costs
Founders' plan: the only positive case, and the only one nobody has run

slides.title: The plan sets all four profit drivers above the best any of our customer sites has reached

claims.claim: The plan sets all four profit drivers above the best any of our customer sites has reached
evidence: Order value: Pop-up $31 | Median $34 | Best site $42 | Plan $45 | Plan gain $2.31 | Plan is 7% above the best site and 45% above the pop-up
Promotions, % of order: 12% | 6% | 6% | 2% | $1.80 | No site runs below 6%; the pop-up needed twice that
Orders per rider-hour: 2.1 | 2.4 | 3 | 3.5 | $2.32 | Above the top of the 1.9–3.0 benchmark range
Orders per site a day: 280 | 900 | 1,400 | 1,800 | $1.75 | Above the top of the 400–1,400 range; the pop-up reached 280
the four gains take the median's −$6.17 to the plan's +$2.02 after site costs

slides.title: No single lever rescues a median site, which would need a $63 basket to break even on order value alone

claims.claim: order value at which a median site breaks even after site costs
evidence: Compared with $42 at the best site and $45 in the plan
Each extra dollar of basket keeps only 21 cents once goods cost and promotions are paid
Bigger baskets cut against the quick top-up order that 15-minute delivery serves

claims.claim: orders per rider-hour a median site would need to break even
evidence: Compared with a benchmark range that tops out at 3.0
Rider cost is the largest per-order cost at the median, above $7 an order
Two of our three launch cities are weighing minimum pay that would raise it
Rider cost per order at the median: $17.75 an hour ÷ 2.4 orders = $7.40

claims.claim: Volume cannot close it: more orders add more loss
evidence: −$2.67 loss per order at the median before any site cost is paid
Store density only spreads the $1.15M fixed cost of a site
With a loss on each order before fixed costs, no level of orders breaks even

slides.title: Zipcart's one profitable city shows what profit cost: a new $3.99 fee, fewer promotions and 14% fewer orders

claims.claim: Losing money nationally, even at scale
evidence: Largest US operator, with $1,200M of revenue in 2025
Lost $1.90 on the average order across its network
Its densest city was the best place to try to turn a profit

claims.claim: Charged customers more and cut discounts
evidence: Added a new $3.99 service fee on every order
Cut promotions to 1% of order value
Did not rely on running stores more efficiently

claims.claim: Impact
evidence: $0.40 contribution per order in the densest city, Q4 2025
$3.99 new service fee charged on every order
−14% change in order volume in that city afterwards

claims.claim: The founders cite it as proof; it shows profit came from charging customers more, at the cost of volume

slides.title: Copying Zipcart's moves would fix the median site's order margin, yet the site would still lose about $1.05 per order

claims.claim: Copying Zipcart's moves would fix the median site's order margin, yet the site would still lose about $1.05 per order
evidence: −$2.67 median site's contribution per order before site costs (14 customer sites, 2025)
+ $3.99 Zipcart's new service fee on every order
+ $1.70 saved by cutting promotions from 6% to 1% of the $34 order
− $4.07 site fixed cost per order once volume falls 14%
= −$1.05 contribution per order after site costs

claims.claim: The estimate is generous to the playbook on four points
evidence: The median customer site's inputs (14 sites, 2025) apply to a Parcelbird store
The full $3.99 service fee is kept, with no extra payment cost on it
Order volume falls 14% as it did in Zipcart's city, and per-order costs stay the same
Rider productivity does not fall with the lower volume (generous to the case)

slides.title: Customers try the service, but few stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost
Stated intent overstates use: only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month three

claims.claim: Stated intent overstates use: only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month three
evidence: Residents who said they would use it weekly 0.44; Pop-up customers still ordering in month three 0.22
Survey of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 (2026) and pop-up customers (autumn 2026)
The survey and the pop-up cover different groups (11,800 orders in six weeks)

claims.claim: The pop-up's growth was bought, and most of it did not stay
evidence: Growth of 18% a week: came with promotions at 12% of order value and first-order credits
Those who stay: order 3.1 times a month, less than once a week

slides.title: Even at the plan's own margins, a retained customer takes about 15 months to repay what it cost to win

claims.claim: Even at the plan's own margins, a retained customer takes about 15 months to repay what it cost to win
evidence: $38 acquisition cost per new customer: paid social and first-order credits (pop-up)
÷ 22% of new customers still ordering in month three (pop-up)
÷ 3.1 orders a month by each retained customer (pop-up)
÷ $3.77 contribution per order before site costs in the founders' plan
= 14.8 months to repay acquisition cost per retained customer

claims.claim: at median economics the cost is never repaid
evidence: At the median site's −$2.67 per order the cost is never repaid

claims.claim: most of the plan's 18-month window passes before a cohort repays its acquisition cost

slides.title: The plan breaches the 12-month runway floor even if everything goes right
Even if every assumption holds, the launch takes our cash below the runway floor the board has set

claims.claim: Even if every assumption holds, the launch takes our cash below the runway floor the board has set
evidence: Cash $M: Cash today 12; Month 18, plan as written 2.5; Month 18, software burn added -4.7
12-month runway floor $4.8M
1.3x the plan's cash need as a multiple of what we can spend while keeping 12 months of runway

claims.claim: Plan as written: what is left covers about 6 months of today's burn, half the floor
Software burn added: if the $9.5M does not include today's burn, cash runs out before month 18
evidence: $12M cash in the bank today − $9.5M founders' plan to month 18 − $7.2M 18 months of today's burn = −$4.7M cash at month 18

claims.claim: No backstop: the lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator "unlikely in this market"

slides.title: At our customers' median economics, nine stores would lose about $18M a year, more than all the cash we hold

claims.claim: At our customers' median economics, nine stores would lose about $18M a year, more than all the cash we hold
evidence: −$6.17 contribution per order after site costs at the median of 14 customer sites
× 328,500 orders per store a year at the median of 900 a day
× 9 dark stores in the founders' plan
= −$18.2M annual operating result of the nine stores

claims.claim: The plan's cash covers its own case only; at median inputs it would be gone within the first year

slides.title: The better path
Nine late-stage grocers alone hold software contracts worth 21% of today's ARR, a far cheaper path to growth

claims.claim: Nine late-stage grocers alone hold software contracts worth 21% of today's ARR
evidence: $0.9M annual contract value of the 9 late-stage grocers
21.1% of today's $4.1M ARR, from late-stage deals alone
Average contract of $96K a year at an 81% gross margin
The full pipeline of 37 grocers is worth $3.55M a year, 87% of today's ARR
On top of ARR already growing 60% a year

claims.claim: Several pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, which our software runs
a far cheaper path to growth
evidence: $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires to scale it
About a twelfth of the plan's $9.5M cash need
The hire cost is about 8% of the plan's cash need ($0.8M ÷ $9.5M)

claims.claim: Keeps grocers as customers instead of turning us into their rival
How long the cash lasts with the hires
evidence: $6.4M cash above the floor of 12 months of the new burn ÷ $466.7K monthly burn (today's $0.4M plus the hires) = 13.7 months until cash meets the floor, with no new contracts

claims.claim: New contracts must start cutting the burn during 2027
evidence: The test investors set: profit within today's cash

slides.title: Scaling the software beats a pilot store, which would spend about $2.6M re-testing what customer sites already show

claims.claim: Launch nine stores: Reject
evidence: Cash needed $9.5M (to month 18)
Keeps 12 months of runway: No: below the floor by month 18 even on plan
Tests: Whether four inputs no site has reached can be hit together

claims.claim: One Columbus store pilot: Reject: little new learning
evidence: Cash needed $2.6M (first year)
Keeps 12 months of runway: No: at today's burn, cash meets the floor within the first year
Tests: What 14 customer sites and our own pop-up already show
$0.6M capex for one dark store + $2.03M first-year operating loss at median inputs, 900 orders a day = $2.6M
at the pop-up's 280 a day it would lose more

claims.claim: Scale the software: Recommend / Grows ARR at an 81% gross margin and keeps grocers as customers, not rivals
evidence: Cash needed $0.8M (a year)
Keeps 12 months of runway: Yes, if new contracts cut the burn during 2027
Tests: Whether grocers buy fast delivery run from their own stores

slides.title: Four conditions, each measurable at our customers' sites, would justify reopening the operator question

claims.claim: A customer site sustains an order value that covers all its costs
evidence: $50.37 to break even at the best site's density and rider speed

claims.claim: New customers stay long enough to repay their cost within a year
evidence: 27.1% still ordering in month three, at plan margins

claims.claim: Rider pay rules are settled in the cities weighing minimum pay
evidence: 2 of our three launch cities are weighing it

claims.claim: Any test is funded only from cash above the board's floor
evidence: $4.8M to hold at all times: 12 months of burn

claims.claim: Our software already sees these numbers at customer sites, so we can watch them without owning a store

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: grow the software business, and reopen the question on four conditions. Scale the software (a year, $0.8M): Recommend — grows ARR at an 81% gross margin and keeps grocers as customers, not rivals.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject: $9.5M cash needed; below the runway floor by month 18 even on plan; tests whether four inputs no site has reached can be hit together
Reject: little new learning; $2.6M cash; at today's burn cash meets the floor within the first year; re-tests what 14 customer sites and the pop-up already show
Recommend: $0.8M; keeps 12 months of runway if new contracts cut the burn during 2027; grows ARR at an 81% gross margin and keeps grocers as customers, not rivals

alternatives_considered.option: Copying Zipcart's playbook ($3.99 fee, promotions cut to 1%)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Would fix the median site's order margin, yet the site would still lose about $1.05 per order

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data from the briefing pack; all figures fictional
Operators' contribution definitions are not disclosed

Zipcart playbook estimate: the median customer site's inputs apply to a Parcelbird store; the full $3.99 fee is kept with no extra payment cost; order volume falls 14% and per-order costs stay the same; rider productivity does not fall with lower volume (generous to the case)
The survey and the pop-up cover different groups: Columbus residents aged 25–39 against customers who placed a pop-up order

Payback: acquisition cost stays at $38; 22% of new customers keep ordering after month three and none leaves later (generous); retained customers order 3.1 times a month at $3.77; orders by customers who leave before month three are not counted
The briefing pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the software business's burn, so both readings are shown; the floor uses today's burn

Nine-store loss: all nine stores run at the median on every input; steady state at 900 orders a day from day one, ramp-up not counted (generous); excludes the $5.4M capex and launch marketing; rider pay stays at $17.75 an hour, minimum pay standards would widen the loss
Software path: 13.7 months until cash meets the floor with no new contracts; new contracts must start cutting the burn during 2027
Pilot loss uses median inputs at 900 orders a day; at the pop-up's 280 a day it would lose more
Reopen thresholds hold the other inputs at the stated values; promotions at the 6% median
Two of our three launch cities are weighing minimum pay that would raise rider cost
next_steps: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch for 2027 and record the four conditions to reopen it — Board — January 2027
Hire 2 engineers and 2 sales staff and close the 9 late-stage grocers — CEO — Q1–Q2 2027
Set a burn plan that keeps 12 months of runway at every month-end — Founders and CFO — Q1 2027
Package fast delivery from existing stores for pipeline grocers — Product and sales — H1 2027
Report the four reopen conditions from customer-site data each quarter — Product analytics — From Q2 2027
